title: What are Spark temporary views (`createOrReplaceTempView` — session-scoped) and global temporary views (`createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` — cross-session, accessed via `global_temp.view_name`), and what are managed vs external/unmanaged tables in Spark (managed = Spark controls data + metadata, drop deletes both; external = Spark controls only metadata, drop keeps data)?
shortTitle: Temporary views, global temporary views, and managed vs external tables

s1_definition.profdef: A temporary view registers a DataFrame under a name so you can query it with Spark SQL, and its scope depends on the kind. A temporary view created with `createOrReplaceTempView` is session-scoped: it lives only within the SparkSession that created it and disappears when that session ends. A global temporary view created with `createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` is tied to the application and visible across sessions, accessed through the reserved `global_temp` database as `global_temp.view_name`. Separately, tables registered in the catalog are either managed or external: for a managed table Spark controls both the data and the metadata, so dropping the table deletes the underlying files, whereas for an external table Spark controls only the metadata and the data lives at a path you specified, so dropping the table removes the catalog entry but leaves the files intact.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India a temporary view is like a sticky note naming a particular report on your own desk — only you, during your current shift (session), can refer to it, and it is gone when you leave. A global temporary view is a sticky note pinned to a shared board in the special "global" corner, so colleagues in other rooms (sessions) of the same building (application) can also refer to it. A managed table is a ledger the bank both owns and stores in its own vault — if the bank discards the ledger entry, the pages are shredded too. An external table is a ledger entry pointing to documents kept in an outside archive the bank only references — discard the entry and the outside documents remain untouched.
s1_definition.oneliner: Temp views are session-scoped names for DataFrames; global temp views are app-wide via global_temp; managed tables let Spark own data and metadata so drop deletes files, while external tables let Spark own only metadata so drop keeps the files.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A temporary view registers a DataFrame under a name so you can query it with Spark SQL, and its scope depends on the kind. A temporary view created with `createOrReplaceTempView` is session-scoped: it lives only within the SparkSession that created it and disappears when that session ends. A global temporary view created with `createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` is tied to the application and visible across sessions, accessed through the reserved `global_temp` database as `global_temp.view_name`. Separately, tables registered in the catalog are either managed or external: for a managed table Spark controls both the data and the metadata, so dropping the table deletes the underlying files, whereas for an external table Spark controls only the metadata and the data lives at a path you specified, so dropping the table removes the catalog entry but leaves the files intact.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India a temporary view is like a sticky note naming a particular report on your own desk — only you, during your current shift (session), can refer to it, and it is gone when you leave. A global temporary view is a sticky note pinned to a shared board in the special "global" corner, so colleagues in other rooms (sessions) of the same building (application) can also refer to it. A managed table is a ledger the bank both owns and stores in its own vault — if the bank discards the ledger entry, the pages are shredded too. An external table is a ledger entry pointing to documents kept in an outside archive the bank only references — discard the entry and the outside documents remain untouched.

**One line to remember:** Temp views are session-scoped names for DataFrames; global temp views are app-wide via global_temp; managed tables let Spark own data and metadata so drop deletes files, while external tables let Spark own only metadata so drop keeps the files.

sections.s2_technical:
A temporary view is a named, queryable handle on a DataFrame, not stored data. createOrReplaceTempView("name") registers the DataFrame's logical plan under that name in the session's catalog, so you can then run spark.sql("SELECT ... FROM name"). It is lazy and virtual: querying the view re-executes the underlying plan, it does not materialize results. Its lifetime is the SparkSession, so another session, even in the same application, cannot see it, and it vanishes when the session closes. You use it to break a complex pipeline into readable SQL steps within one job.

A global temporary view extends the scope to the whole Spark application. createOrReplaceGlobalTempView("name") registers it in a special system-preserved database called global_temp, and any session in the same application can query it as global_temp.name. You must include the global_temp qualifier, because the view is not in the current session's default database. This is useful when multiple sessions within one application, such as different threads or notebook contexts sharing a SparkContext, need to share a view. Like a temporary view it is still virtual and disappears when the application ends.

Managed tables, also called internal tables, are tables where Spark owns both the metadata in the catalog and the data files in the warehouse location. You create one with saveAsTable without specifying an external path, and Spark places the files under the warehouse directory. Because Spark owns the data, DROP TABLE deletes both the catalog entry and the underlying files. Managed tables are convenient when Spark is the system of record for that data and its lifecycle should follow the table.

External tables, also called unmanaged tables, are tables where you point the catalog at data living at a specific path you control, using an explicit location. Spark records the metadata but does not own the files. DROP TABLE removes only the catalog entry; the data files remain at the path. External tables are the right choice when the data is shared with other tools, when it existed before Spark and must survive table drops, or when you want full control over the physical layout and lifecycle. A senior-level nuance is that the managed-versus-external choice is fundamentally about data ownership and blast radius: in a bank, accidentally dropping a managed table can irrecoverably delete regulated data, so critical shared datasets are almost always external with the files protected independently, while managed tables are reserved for data whose existence truly should be bound to the table. You also keep in mind that views are virtual and cost nothing to store but re-run their plan each query, whereas tables persist data; choosing a temp view versus a cached DataFrame versus a persisted table is a trade-off between recomputation, memory, and durability that you make deliberately.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India breaks a reporting job into readable SQL steps within one session using temporary views for intermediate results that need no persistence.

Problem 2 — Two cooperating sessions in the same application need to share a filtered view of high-value transactions, so a global temporary view in global_temp is used.

Problem 3 — A regulated transactions dataset must survive even if someone drops the table definition, so it is registered as an external table pointing at a protected path, whereas a scratch aggregate that should vanish with its table is managed.

The demo models a simple catalog that registers session temp views, global temp views, and managed versus external tables, and shows what a drop does to each — deleting files only for the managed table — logging the outcomes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four catalog registrations — a session temp view, a global temp view, a managed table owning its data, and an external table pointing at a protected path.

Step 1: The temp view dailyStep is registered under its plain name. The global temp view highValue is registered under the qualified name global_temp.highValue, reflecting that it lives in the special global database.

Step 2: Visibility is checked across a simulated other session. The temp view is not visible in another session because it is session-scoped. The global temp view is visible because it is application-scoped.

Step 3: The managed table scratchAgg is dropped. Because Spark owns its data, the drop deletes the underlying files, logged as a warning that data files were deleted.

Step 4: The external table regulatedTxns is dropped, removing only its metadata and keeping the data files at the protected path, and finally the temp view is dropped, which is virtual and has no data to delete. The outcomes show the central difference: only the managed-table drop destroys data.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  DataFrame / data
    │
    ├─ createOrReplaceTempView ──────→ session catalog   (scope: THIS session)
    │
    ├─ createOrReplaceGlobalTempView ─→ global_temp db   (scope: whole APP)
    │        query as: global_temp.name
    │
    ├─ saveAsTable (no path) ─────────→ MANAGED table (Spark owns data)
    │        DROP → metadata gone + DATA FILES DELETED
    │
    └─ saveAsTable (explicit path) ───→ EXTERNAL table (you own data)
             DROP → metadata gone, DATA FILES KEPT
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Temporary views and global temporary views are named, queryable handles on DataFrames, differing in scope. A temporary view created with createOrReplaceTempView is session-scoped: it lives only in the SparkSession that created it, is invisible to other sessions even in the same application, and vanishes when the session ends. A global temporary view created with createOrReplaceGlobalTempView is application-scoped: it is registered in a special system database called global_temp and any session in the same application can query it, but you must qualify the name as global_temp dot the view name. Both are virtual — they re-execute their underlying plan on each query rather than storing data — so they cost nothing to keep but recompute each time.

Managed and external tables, by contrast, are catalog-registered tables that persist data, and they differ in who owns that data. A managed table, created with saveAsTable without an explicit location, is one where Spark owns both the metadata and the data files under the warehouse directory, so dropping the table deletes the files too. An external table, created by pointing at an explicit path, is one where Spark owns only the metadata and the data lives at a path you control, so dropping the table removes the catalog entry but leaves the files intact. The choice is fundamentally about data ownership and blast radius.

At the National Bank of India I used temporary views to break reporting jobs into readable SQL steps within a session, a global temporary view when two cooperating sessions in one application needed to share a filtered high-value-transactions view, and I was deliberate about managed versus external tables. Regulated and shared datasets were always external tables pointing at protected paths, because an accidental drop of a managed table would irrecoverably delete regulated data, while managed tables were reserved for scratch aggregates whose existence genuinely should be bound to the table. The rule I give in interviews is: temp views for session-local SQL steps, global temp views to share across sessions in one app, managed tables when Spark should own the data lifecycle, and external tables for shared or regulated data that must survive a table drop.
